udocker is unrelated to the Docker socket. You can run udocker inside Docker.

udocker is currently supported for CentOS, RH, Fedora, Ubuntu.
Execution of udocker inside Alpine is currently not supported, but feedback or contributions are welcome.

Having said you can try the following once inside the alpine container running in Docker.

apk update
apk add curl
curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/indigo-dc/udocker/devel/udocker.py > udocker
chmod a+rx udocker
 
apk add python
apk add tar
apk add findutils
apk add file
./udocker --allow-root install

Now to run a centos6 container:

./udocker --allow-root pull ubuntu:16
./udocker --allow-root create --name=c6 centos:centos6
./udocker --allow-root setup --execmode=F1 c6
./udocker --allow-root run --nosysdirs  c6


Notice that running an Alpine container inside udocker itself does not yet work in 
the Fn execution modes which are the only ones that can work inside Docker.
The default Pn modes do support Alpine containers execution but unfortunately
 these modes require PTRACE which does not work inside Docker. We are 
working to support Alpine containers execution in the Fn modes.

Docker (not udocker) tries hard to prevent processes inside containers to gain access to the host, several functionalities needed by the P1 and P2 modes of udocker are disabled by default in Docker. You can try to use the Fn modes  as explained in https://github.com/indigo-dc/udocker/issues/106 or
Start Docker (not udocker) as a privileged container like: run --privileged.

@jorge-lip running as privilged would be a bad idea, I would still go with by just giving it access to the required syscalls, but running in Fn mode kind of solved my problem, as I'm not trying to run udocker as fully isolated in a container, but at least some namespace separation. This issue may be closed if you feel so, a big thanks for the maintainers on the prompt and fast response. It would be great if a section be added in README on how to run udocker inside a container with the required dependencies.

Sure, if you want some level of separation/protection and really want to use Docker then you should run udocker inside Docker with the Fn modes. The udocker R1 mode uses runC and user level namespaces thus also providing some separation (currently not as complete as Docker). With this mode you may be able to run and have separation without using Docker, but only works in very recent kernels (notably does not work with CentOS 6 and 7).

Hi @jorge-lip, It is a problem with the url redirection made when downloading the layers. This error appears: ```xml InvalidArgument Only one auth mechanism allowed; only the X-Amz-Algorithm query parameter, Signature query string parameter or the Authorization header should be specified Authorization Bearer .... ... ... ``` When curl/pycurl performs the redirection it maintains the headers of the original request. In case of S3 it includes some parameters in the url ("Signature") for the authentication so the "Authentication" header must be removed to make it work correctly. We don't know why it only fails inside AWS resources ... I have proposed a fix in our fork.

udocker create --name=myc ${CNAME}
udocker run myc

For me it appears that `useradd` works in Ubuntu. However, it's of little use as the host filesystem always has the user which ran the container as the owner of all the files in the container folder. So basically `useradd -m foo` works, but` ls -l /home` shows that `/home/foo` belongs to `root`. Now it's possible to do `su - foo` in the container, but under foo `ls /` magically shows that `/bin` belongs to `foo` now. 

I think these are fundamental limitations of the rootless approach, and we need a chroot-based engine which will require root but won't require the namespaces and other kernel features we don't have in CentOS 6.

The Pn and Fn modes are completely different and without further information is very difficult to understand what might be affecting both. For Fn we know of situations where pathname translation for "mounted" directories may fail. The fixes for these will be in the next release. However the situation you mention seems random and more related to the load. 

If you plan to dig in please focus on the Fn execution modes.

There are no "mounts" in udocker just pathname translations. For the Fn modes mapping of pathnames is passed via environment variables to the LD_PRELOAD shareable library that intercepts the calls.
There are two env variables used FAKECHROOT_DIR_MAP which maps a host pathname to a container pathname and FAKECHROOT_EXCLUDE_PATH that simply allows the passthrough of pathnames that are common between the host and the container (eg map /home in the host to /home in the container). You can check if these mappings are ok. There is a maximum of 64 map entries for each of the methods. Since Fn uses a preload library it also consumes a bit more memory.

It's a known problem of centos6 - it has an old kernel incompatible with newer glibc.

It's likely that the image wasn't built against the older `glibc` in CentOS 6. "Kernel too old" comes from glibc in the image, mostly because it doesn't find necessary syscalls (e.g. `openat`)

Also the kernel seems too old even for centos 6 - the recent version is 754.14.2.el6

Also make sure you are not on OpenVZ 6 - it has pretty old kernel so it's really hard these days to run any software there.

Your solution is to recompile the glibc in the images so it supports 2.6.32. Fortunately recent glibc doesn't support the generic 2.6.32 kernel, but it does support the heavily patched 2.6.32 which comes with CentOS 6

The default behavior of udocker is starting Pn as root and Sn as normal user. We don't want to change that, as this is what the users expect as default behavior. Defaults will likely change for udocker3.

udocker uses the tar command from the host system and produces  "Error: while extracting image layer" when tar returns a non-zero value. This can have different reasons such as:
a) problems like file system full or insufficient permissions  
b) limitations in tar or in commands invoked by tar like in the handling of sparse file formats 
c) extracting content that cannot be extracted by non-root users like creating devices. 
Notice that in most cases the errors are non fatal and the extraction continues until the end, depending on the actual reason this error might be irrelevant or important. 

When such errors occur the current solution is to recreate the container with debug as in `udocker -D create IMAGE` search for the actual tar errors and see if they are relevant for the container execution .e.g. `udocker -D create IMAGE 2>&1 | grep  '^tar.*:'`

According to comments, we moved the focus to the Python 3 version which is now in the master branch,
and we also released version 1.3.0. As recommended the documentation has been improved including 
the README, user manual and installation manual. The rendering of the documentation is now performed 
with a jekyll frontend.

Regarding the root concerns we changed the security section in the documentation making it clearer that 
we are not breaking anything in the system  https://github.com/indigo-dc/udocker#security

udocker enables execution without using namespaces or any other of the kernel functionalities required by Singularity or 
Podman. Also does not require privileges to execute. Many sites refuse to support Singularity due to the past security 
vulnerabilities. We have many users from the life sciences community where security and privacy are a concern.

With the udocker default execution mode you can even execute applications compiled for the latest kernels and libc
in systems as old as CentOS 6, where supposedly you would get a kernel too old message when using other solutions.
The fakechroot based mode of udocker is also in many cases faster than other containerization solutions.

The tool also does not require compilation or system installation making it ideal to execute in remote clusters and
grid infrastructures as you can submit udocker with the batch job.

Notice that computer clusters are usually conservative they run with OSes like CentOS 7 using batch systems like 
Slurm. In such environment you likely don't have the user namespace enabled, meaning that containerized solutions
like Singularity need to be installed by the sysadmins with privileges. So if Singularity is not installed you will not be
able to run containers.

Being able to use a single solution across systems is also very important when you are using multiple computing
clusters with different characteristics and configurations. It provides a common basis for the execution of the 
applications across these heterogeneous environments. The EGI infrastructure www.egi.eu and several of its user 
communities are using  udocker to support execution of containers in batch systems in computing clusters across 
Europe.

udocker is also unique in supporting multiple execution modes (using different tools) to give the best chances of 
running applications across different environments. We revised the documentation, hopefully the advantages and
characteristics are now more clear.

The have unit tests, integration tests, security tests with bandit and code style checking. We use Jenkins pipelines for our SQA.

A comparison with Shifter and Sarus was added to the paper. They have different focus/constraints, while udocker main goal is to provide a runtime to execute containers without requiring privileges or installation by the systems administrator, these other tools require privileges and installation by the system administrator. The functionalities udocker are consequently limited to what can be achieved without privileges. On the other hand udocker does not pose the privilege escalation risks.
The tools used are now listed in tables in section 6 of the installation manual together with the repositories and licenses.

The Apache License 2.0 is for udocker only, the other tools retain their original licenses and we make the source code changes public. What is done by udocker is not different than a Linux distro does by distributing multiple software with multiple licenses. The problem with mixed licenses arises typically when a single indivisible object incorporates code with multiple licenses. That is not the case of udocker itself that is a Python script and is not linked against those other codes.
Many thanks for the suggestions we will address those in a future release.

As I've said, I am not sure myself.
Basically a user must be aware which licenses he must regard if going further than personal use, especially in case of redistribution. This is one reason why I've insisted on a list of licenses and origin of `udocker-tools`. 

A quick solution would be a hint like:
_"Redistribution, commercial use and code changes must regard all licenses shipped with udocker."_ (edited)
This is formally correct and likely enough, but leaves it up to the user to figure out the consequences himself.

It would help the user to give some hints on the consequences. Though, I can't tell the consequences myself, I am not an expert in interfering software licenses. (Is _anyone_ an expert in this?)

Agree I have added the suggested statement to the README, to the introduction of the installation manual and also in the licenses section of the installation manual. The full statement is:

Redistribution, commercial use and code changes must regard all licenses shipped with udocker. These include the udocker license and the individual licences of the external tools and libraries packaged for use
with udocker. For further information see the [software licenses section](https://indigo-dc.github.io/udocker/installation_manual.html#62-software-licenses) of the installation manual.

Since 1.1.1, udocker moved from a proof of concept tool suitable for production. The focus has been put on sustainability and interoperability. The code structure was redesigned moving from the Python 2 monolithic code to a new Python 3 modular implementation. New features and improvements were added to support a wider range of Linux distributions and environments. To this end the execution engines now support `crun` for namespace based execution with `cgroups v2` and a port of `Fakechroot` to support `MUSL libc`. The existing execution engines were also enhanced to address the shortcomings present in the proof of concept and improve interoperability for execution across a wider range of distributions, kernels and better supporting the functionalities required for containers execution.  Support for multiple architectures was added and binaries for ARM and x86 are now provided for `PRoot` based execution, further binaries can be easily added as needed. Support for accelerated computing was implemented by introducing the capability to setup containers to use NVIDIA GPUs according to the host environment and across the several execution engines. The handling of container images was improved both at the level of interaction with container registries and handling of formats. The interaction with registries is now more interoperable and robust and support for the OCI image specification v1 was introduced. Furthermore the search capabilities support docker registry v1 and v2 specifications and listing of tags. The command line interface and configuration was improved with new commands, flags and better parsing of both the command line and config files. Finally the installation of the tools and libraries was decoupled from udocker itself, both can now be released separately. The shared installation of udocker in distributed filesystems was addressed with changes introduced to handle the cases where udocker is executed from readonly filesystems. Finally, udocker is now also available from *PyPI*. A more complete description is provided in the paper.

This is a by design limitation of running with F1 and F2 not an issue. Modes F1 and F2 are meant to be fast to setup requiring very few changes to the container content at the expense of potential library loading related problems. On the other hand with mode F3 these application errors are much less likely to happen but at the expense of potentially painfully slow setup times especially when the container files are in distributed/remote file systems as mode F3 needs to make changes to the ELF headers of all executables and shared libraries precisely to avoid the problems that may arise with F1 and F2.

Bottom line depending on the application the modes F1 or F2 may work just fine, if they don't please use F3.

udocker uses a modified libfakechroot library. The library must be compiled against the libc of the container.
Possibly the version of udocker used here didn't had the right version of the libfakechroot library.

Recent versions of udocker should have the correct library for Debian 11.
Also notice that depending on the application this may also happen when using modes other than F3 or F4.
This  is was implemented in the latest versions of udocker.

In the latest commit, I tried to let udocker add NVIDIA library path to `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` before running a container(if nvidia mode is set).  

* In udocker container, NVIDIA library path could be  `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu`  or  `/usr/lib64`.  

Although `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` and `/usr/lib64` are common default locations for the linker to find libraries, some programs still detect the environment depending on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.    

For example, when using the image mentioned in #425 (pytorch/pytorch:2.5.1-cuda12.4-cudnn9-runtime), the container created from it will throw a WARNING message upon startup:  

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1dc4ebb0-921c-4bd1-96b5-a30b9b782391)

By checking the entrypoint scripts, I found that the issue mainly arises from the absence of the library path mentioned above in `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`. (Or `ldconfig -p` not updated, but it's not common to run `ldconfig` while starting a container)  

After the fix, it won't print the warning message anymore:  

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/de85a483-fb31-4d5b-8553-77e606cfe845)

----

In my test, without this commit, PyTorch can still access GPU normally(It may use default searching locations). But I'm not sure if there are applications that mainly depend on the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` to detect the libraries. In any case, at least this can help avoid some warning messages, and it won't disrupt the search for shared libraries.
